12 A tennis ball is thrown vertically upwards. The tennis ball reaches its highest point and then falls
back down to the point from which it was thrown.
Air resistance is significant.
At which position on the path of the tennis ball is the resultant force on the tennis ball greatest?
A
at the start just after the tennis ball is released
B
when the tennis ball is halfway to its highest point on the way up
C
when the tennis ball is at its highest point
D
when the tennis ball is halfway from its highest point on the way down

hints: Identify the two forces throughout the flight: constant weight downwards and air resistance always opposite to velocity.
Compare directions: on the way up weight and drag add, at the top drag is zero, and on the way down drag subtracts from weight.
Recall that significant air resistance increases with speed, so ask at which listed position the upward speed of the tennis ball is largest.
walkthrough: List the forces: weight $W = mg$ acts vertically down at all positions, and drag $D$ acts opposite to velocity with magnitude increasing as speed increases.
On the way up velocity is up so drag is down. The resultant downward force is $F_{res} = W + D$.
At the highest point velocity is instantaneously zero, so $D = 0$ and $F_{res} = W$.
On the way down velocity is down so drag is up. The resultant downward force is $F_{res} = W - D$, which is less than $W$.
Speed on the way up is greatest just after release and then decreases to zero at the top, so $D$ and hence $W + D$ are greatest at the start.
Therefore the greatest resultant force is just after release on the way up. This is option A.

A.explanation: On the way up weight and air resistance both act downwards, and speed and so drag are largest just after release, giving $F_{res} = W + D_{max}$.

B.explanation: The ball is slower halfway up than at release, so drag is smaller and $W + D$ is smaller than at the start.

C.explanation: At the highest point velocity is zero so drag is zero and resultant force is just weight $W$.

D.explanation: On the way down drag acts upwards, so resultant force $W - D$ is less than weight and less than on the way up.
